title: The Chipko Movement
text:
In the early 1970s villagers in the Garhwal Himalaya, then part of Uttar Pradesh in India, watched commercial contractors fell the forests their lives depended on for fuel, fodder and water, while their own requests to use the trees were refused. In 1973 the forest department denied a local cooperative, led by Chandi Prasad Bhatt, a few ash trees for making farm tools, but granted ash trees in the same area to a sporting goods company. The villagers of Mandal said that if the loggers came, they would hug the trees. The loggers left without cutting.

The most famous confrontation came on 26 March 1974 near the village of Reni. The men of the village had gone to the district town to receive compensation for land, and the contractors' workers arrived to cut the forest. Gaura Devi, a widow who led the local women's group, gathered other women and girls and went into the forest. They stood between the workers and the trees and refused to move. After a long standoff, the loggers withdrew.

The word chipko means "to cling" or "to embrace." The movement spread across the hills, with women at its center, and the activist Sunderlal Bahuguna carried its message across India. In 1980 the central government banned commercial felling of green trees in the Himalayan forests of Uttar Pradesh for fifteen years.
lesson: People acting together nonviolently can protect what they share. When those most affected organize, they often prove more powerful than they seem.
people: Gaura Devi, Chandi Prasad Bhatt, Sunderlal Bahuguna, villagers of Mandal and Reni
caveat: Popular retellings simplify the movement; tree hugging was more a threat and symbol than a literal tactic at every action.
